```{r}
#| label: prepare
#| include: false
# ---- 1988: how many towers in each settlement type -------------------------
# The 1988 report does not publish the counts. They are inferred from Table
# 11.2 (shared bands), which gives two percentages per type: the type's share
# of the 47 towers with shared bands, and the share of the type's own towers
# with a shared band. Rounding leaves a range for each count. See the prose.
counts_1988 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~type_1988,   ~shared_pct_of_47, ~shared,  ~pct_within, ~n_min, ~n_max, ~n_best,
  "Inner City",  9,                 4,        50,           8,      8,      8,
  "Suburban",    9,                 4,         9,          43,     47,     45,
  "Large City",  4,                 2,         9,          22,     23,     23,
  "Town",       26,                12,        11,         105,    114,    110,
  "Village",    53,                25,        12,         201,    217,    209
)
share_range <- function(i) {
  lo <- counts_1988$n_min[i] / (counts_1988$n_min[i] + sum(counts_1988$n_max[-i]))
  hi <- counts_1988$n_max[i] / (counts_1988$n_max[i] + sum(counts_1988$n_min[-i]))
  c(lo, hi)
}
counts_1988 <- counts_1988 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    share_best = .data$n_best / sum(.data$n_best),
    share_lo   = purrr::map_dbl(dplyr::row_number(), \(i) share_range(i)[1]),
    share_hi   = purrr::map_dbl(dplyr::row_number(), \(i) share_range(i)[2])
  )
TYPES_1988 <- counts_1988$type_1988

# 1988 Tables 9.1-9.3, by settlement type.
rates_1988 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~type_1988,   ~rung_pct, ~band_pct, ~ringers_per_bell,
  "Inner City",  63,        63,        1.22,
  "Suburban",    80,        92,        1.45,
  "Large City",  83,        92,        1.70,
  "Town",        81,        92,        1.42,
  "Village",     46,        70,        1.24
)

# Draft A's mapping to 1988, as used in the earlier draft.
crosswalk_1988_a <- c(
  "Village"                             = "Village",
  "Village in a built-up region"        = "Village",
  "Town"                                = "Town",
  "Town in a built-up region"           = "Suburban",
  "City or large town"                  = "Large City",
  "City or large town in a conurbation" = "Inner City",
  "Society or city-core tower"          = "Inner City"
)

# Share of comparable towers in each 1988 type, under each draft. Built
# directly rather than with summarise(), which no longer accepts a result of
# more than one row per group.
share_1988_types <- function(types, crosswalk) {
  as.numeric(prop.table(table(factor(unname(crosswalk[as.character(types)]),
                                     levels = TYPES_1988))))
}
shares_vs_1988 <- tibble::tibble(
  type_1988 = TYPES_1988,
  draft_a   = share_1988_types(comparable_1988$type_a, crosswalk_1988_a),
  draft_c   = as.numeric(prop.table(table(factor(comparable_1988$type_1988, levels = TYPES_1988))))
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(counts_1988 |> dplyr::select("type_1988", "share_best", "share_lo", "share_hi"),
                   by = "type_1988")
village_a <- shares_vs_1988$draft_a[shares_vs_1988$type_1988 == "Village"]
village_c <- shares_vs_1988$draft_c[shares_vs_1988$type_1988 == "Village"]
village_88 <- counts_1988$share_best[counts_1988$type_1988 == "Village"]

# ---- independent checks on Draft C -----------------------------------------
ring_check <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::summarise(towers = dplyr::n(), p8 = mean(.data$bells >= 8),
                   `median growth since bells (u)` = round(stats::median(.data$u), 2),
                   .by = "type") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$type)
p8_of <- \(t) ring_check$p8[ring_check$type == t]

# ---- known towers -------------------------------------------------------------
# known_towers.csv records feelings in the older, simpler words. Each maps
# onto the types it agrees with: a city's or a conurbation's centre is "a
# city", either kind of suburb is "Suburban".
FEELS_AGREE <- list(
  "Small village or hamlet" = "Small village or hamlet",
  "Village"                 = "Village",
  "Town"                    = "Town",
  "City or large town"      = c("City or large town: centre", "Conurbation: centre"),
  "Suburban"                = c("City or large town: suburb", "Conurbation: suburb"),
  "Inner city"              = "Conurbation: centre"
)
agrees <- function(feels, type) {
  purrr::map2_lgl(feels, as.character(type), \(f, t) t %in% FEELS_AGREE[[f]])
}
known_c <- known |>
  dplyr::select("tower_id", "known_by", "relationship", "feels_like", "why") |>
  dplyr::inner_join(towers, by = "tower_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(agree = agrees(.data$feels_like, .data$type))
n_known_missing <- nrow(known) - nrow(known_c)
known_row <- \(id) dplyr::filter(known_c, .data$tower_id == id)
welwyn    <- known_row("14639")
amersham  <- known_row("14913")
staines   <- known_row("11525")
st_albans <- known_row("15782")

# ---- reclassify with one threshold changed (for sensitivity tables) ---------
# Retail nearness is recomputed from the thresholds, so the retail tier and
# distance can be varied too. local: the density that sets town and village.
reclass <- function(d, ..., local = LOCAL_VAR) {
  th <- utils::modifyList(DRAFT_C, list(...))
  near <- retail_near(dplyr::select(d, dplyr::starts_with("retail_d_t")), th)
  classify_settlement_c(d$centre_key, d$centre_pop, d[[local]], near, d$nres_ratio,
                        d$towers_1km, d$in_frame, th, TYPE_LEVELS)
}
# Shares of comparable towers in 1988's three urban types, for a set of types
# given for every frame tower.
urban_88 <- function(type) {
  keep <- frame_towers$tower_id %in% comparable_1988$tower_id
  t88 <- ifelse(frame_towers$tower_cluster, "Large City",
                unname(crosswalk_1988[as.character(type)]))[keep]
  c(`Large City` = mean(t88 == "Large City"), Suburban = mean(t88 == "Suburban"),
    `Inner City` = mean(t88 == "Inner City"))
}
# The town line at which Draft C's town share comes closest to 1988's.
town_88 <- counts_1988$share_best[counts_1988$type_1988 == "Town"]
town_c  <- shares_vs_1988$draft_c[shares_vs_1988$type_1988 == "Town"]
line_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(300, 1500, by = 50), DRAFT_C$town_density)))
town_share_at <- purrr::map_dbl(line_grid, \(t)
  mean(reclass(comparable_1988, town_density = t) == "Town"))
line_88 <- line_grid[which.min(abs(town_share_at - town_88))]
village_c_at_88 <- mean(reclass(comparable_1988, town_density = line_88) %in%
                          c("Village", "Small village or hamlet"))

# ---- how centres are found: evidence for the rule (D-036, D-037) -----------
# Test cases chosen by Mark and Claude before either rule was settled:
# churches at the heart of their towns, and churches in suburbs.
TEST_CENTRES <- c("Wolverhampton, Collegiate", "Rotherham, Minster", "Halifax, Minster",
                  "St Helens, Minster", "Shrewsbury, S Chad", "Warwick, S Mary", "Solihull",
                  "Kingston upon Hull, HT", "Carlisle Cath", "Pontefract, S Giles",
                  "Dudley, S Thomas", "Basingstoke, All", "Fareham", "Poole, S James",
                  "Leyland", "Epsom, S Martin", "Waltham Abbey", "St Albans Cath",
                  "Colchester, S Peter", "Hastings, All", "Wakefield Cath",
                  "Cheltenham, S Mary", "Luton, S Mary", "Exeter Cath", "Gloucester Cath",
                  "Stafford, S Mary", "Watford, S Mary", "Stockport, S George",
                  "Kingston upon Thames", "Croydon", "Bristol Cath", "Birmingham, S Martin",
                  "Manchester Cath", "Stevenage")
TEST_SUBURBS <- c("Barnwood", "Dunstable", "Charlton Kings", "Staines, S Peter", "Quedgeley",
                  "Brockworth", "Prestbury", "Leckhampton", "Shrub End", "St Albans, S Stephen",
                  "Upton St Leonards", "King's Norton", "Worsley", "Dunham Massey",
                  "Northfield", "Hanwell", "Eltham", "Harraby", "Wimbledon", "Ossett",
                  "Mirfield")
matches_any <- \(d, names) vapply(d$display, \(x)
  any(startsWith(x, names) | grepl(paste0(", ", names), x, fixed = TRUE)), TRUE)
in_c <- !is.na(frame_towers$centre_pop)
is_test_centre <- in_c & matches_any(frame_towers, TEST_CENTRES)
is_test_suburb <- in_c & matches_any(frame_towers, TEST_SUBURBS)
# Each rule gives every frame tower a type. The first three compare the area
# round the church with its own urban centre (retail centres switched off, so
# the comparison decides everywhere); the rest use retail centres.
no_retail <- \(d) dplyr::mutate(d, dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("retail_d_t"), \(x) NA_real_))
CHOSEN_RULE <- "District Centre or larger within 250 m (Draft C)"
centre_rules <- list(
  "People per km² of land, against its built-up area's" = \(d)
    reclass(no_retail(dplyr::mutate(d, nres_ratio = .data[[LOCAL_VAR]] /
                                      (.data$centre_pop / .data$centre_km2)))),
  "Share of land built on, against its built-up area's" = \(d)
    reclass(no_retail(dplyr::mutate(d, nres_ratio = (.data$built_km2_k500m / .data$land_km2_k500m) /
                                      (.data$centre_built_km2 / .data$centre_km2)))),
  "Non-residential share of buildings, against its built-up area's (Draft B)" = \(d)
    reclass(no_retail(d)),
  "Town Centre or larger within 250 m" = \(d) reclass(d, centre_retail_tier = 3),
  "District Centre or larger within 250 m (Draft C)" = \(d) reclass(d),
  "District Centre or larger within 400 m" = \(d) reclass(d, centre_retail_m = 400),
  "Local Centre or larger within 250 m" = \(d) reclass(d, centre_retail_tier = 5)
)
short <- \(m) paste(sub(",.*$", "", frame_towers$display[m]), collapse = ", ")
centre_types <- purrr::map(centre_rules, \(f) f(frame_towers))
centre_test <- purrr::imap(centre_types, \(type, name) {
  central <- !grepl("suburb", type)
  u <- urban_88(type)
  tibble::tibble(rule = name,
                 `Large City` = pct(u[["Large City"]]), Suburban = pct(u[["Suburban"]]),
                 `Inner City` = pct(u[["Inner City"]]),
                 `centres made suburbs` = sum(is_test_centre & !central),
                 `the centres` = short(is_test_centre & !central),
                 `suburbs made centres` = sum(is_test_suburb & central),
                 `the suburbs` = short(is_test_suburb & central))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
ct <- \(rule, col) centre_test[[col]][centre_test$rule == rule]
known_agree_under <- function(type) {
  k <- match(known_c$tower_id, frame_towers$tower_id)
  sum(agrees(known_c$feels_like, type[k]), na.rm = TRUE)
}
known_by_rule <- purrr::map_int(centre_types, known_agree_under)
n_extra_local <- sum(grepl("centre", centre_types[["Local Centre or larger within 250 m"]]) &
                       !grepl("centre", frame_towers$type))
staines_at <- \(rule) as.character(centre_types[[rule]][frame_towers$tower_id == "11525"])

# ---- the town scale ------------------------------------------------------------
# Each kernel's town line is set to match 1988's share of towns, then each is
# checked against the contiguous urban clusters (5,000+ people), traced
# without any kernel. Kept to show why that check misleads: see the prose.
town_line_for <- function(var) {
  grid <- signif(stats::quantile(comparable_1988[[var]], seq(0.3, 0.9, by = 0.005), na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  grid <- sort(unique(grid))
  share <- purrr::map_dbl(grid, \(t) mean(reclass(comparable_1988, town_density = t,
                                                 village_density = 0, local = var) == "Town"))
  grid[which.min(abs(share - town_88))]
}
rural_bi <- dplyr::filter(frame_towers, .data$british_isles, is.na(.data$centre_pop))
town_scale <- tibble::tibble(
  kernel = c("250 m", "500 m", "1 km", "2 km"),
  var = paste0("density_land_k", c("250m", "500m", "1km", "2km"))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(line = purrr::map_dbl(.data$var, town_line_for),
                agree = purrr::map2_dbl(.data$var, .data$line, \(v, l)
                  mean((rural_bi[[v]] >= l) == !is.na(rural_bi$urban_pop))))
# Three Hertfordshire villages Mark knows, and the town between them.
HERTS <- c("Codicote", "Datchworth", "Tewin", "Welwyn")
herts <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(sub(",.*$", "", .data$display) %in% HERTS) |>
  dplyr::distinct(.data$tower_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

*Prepared by Mark Ainsworth with Claude (Anthropic). Mark set the questions
and made the decisions; Claude drafted the code and text, which Mark
reviewed.*

## Where this stands

*Mark's take, drafted by Claude from Mark's decisions. Tentative: to be
tested with the other analysis volunteers.*

**Current recommendation.** Use Draft C to describe every tower and to
stratify the chased sample. It answers "what sort of place are these bells
in?" from place measures alone, in seven types. Towers in a tower cluster
(`r fmt(DRAFT_C$cluster_towers)` or more towers within 1 km) are flagged
on top of their type:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stand
frame_towers |>
  dplyr::count(.data$type, name = "frame towers") |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(.data$`frame towers` / sum(.data$`frame towers`))) |>
  dplyr::left_join(tibble::tibble(
    type = factor(TYPE_LEVELS, levels = TYPE_LEVELS),
    `in plain words` = c(
      paste0("Under ", fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density), " people per km² of land within a short walk of the church"),
      paste0(fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density), " to ", fmt(DRAFT_C$town_density), " people per km² of land within a short walk of the church"),
      paste0(fmt(DRAFT_C$town_density), "+ people per km² of land within a short walk of the church, outside any city"),
      paste0("In a continuous built-up area of 50,000 to ", fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop), " people, away from its centre"),
      "In the centre of that built-up area: on or by its high street, or among its old churches",
      paste0("In a continuous built-up area of ", fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop), " people or more, away from a centre"),
      "In one of a conurbation's centres, by the same test"
    )), by = "type") |>
  dplyr::select("type", "in plain words", "frame towers", "share") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**Settled so far** (decision log D-028, D-029, D-033 to D-037):

- Place measures only. Ring size checks the types but never defines them.
- Cities, suburbs and conurbations come from the continuous built-up area,
  so St Albans (its own city) and Staines (part of London) fall apart.
- Outside cities, towns and villages are lines of density: people per km²
  of land within a short walk of the church (the 250 m kernel). A wider
  kernel picks up the next village, and made villages such as Datchworth and
  Tewin into towns. The town line is close to 1988's share of towns.
- Inside a built-up area, a tower is in a **centre** if it stands on or
  within `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m of a high street of District Centre
  size or larger, as mapped by the Consumer Data Research Centre (CDRC).
  Old centres of churches count too, and every settlement has at least one
  centre. Every other tower is in a **suburb**. Abroad, where no retail
  centres are mapped, the non-residential share of buildings decides
  instead.
- The names are neutral: centre or suburb, of a conurbation or of a city or
  large town. Nobody's church is graded by a prestigious title.
- **Tower clusters** are a flag, not a type: `r fmt(DRAFT_C$cluster_towers)`
  or more towers within 1 km, the tower itself included, close enough for one
  band to ring several in a morning.
- The conurbation line sits in a gap between city sizes, with Bristol inside.
- Two measures are kept beside the types but play no part in them: the
  density *beyond* a short walk (between the 250 m and 2 km kernels), which
  says how isolated a place is and sorts the draw within each stratum; and
  the non-residential share of buildings.
- Aligning with 1988's five types is a high priority, given the standing of
  their author.

**Still open.**

1. *Validation.* The lines rest on a few dozen test towers, a dozen known
   towers, inferred 1988 shares, and one Association's register. Volunteers'
   known towers, recorded before they see the class, would test them
   properly.
2. *Town centres the retail map misses.* `r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "centres made suburbs")`
   of `r sum(is_test_centre)` test centres come out as suburbs
   (`r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "the centres")`): their church sits more than
   `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m from the mapped high street, or the CDRC
   files it as a smaller centre.
3. *Suburban is still below 1988's share*
   (`r pct(mean(grepl("suburb", comparable_1988$type)))` against 11%).
4. *The special-case list* (Q-022): now a backstop to the tower-cluster
   flag; its society and university-society rows still need confirming.

## Background and brief

**Where this fits.** The census will chase about 1,000 randomly drawn towers
until each replies. The draw, and every later analysis, needs a way of saying
what sort of place each tower is in. The chapter *Towers and the places they
stand in* built and explored the measures, and *What the bells remember*
looked at how ring size relates to them. This chapter turns them into
named place types. *Choosing a sampling method* then uses the types.

**What Mark asked for.**

- *One question, answered clearly:* "what sort of place are these bells
  in?" Clarity of the concept, and of how it is communicated, comes first.
- *Place only, never bells.* The types will be crossed with ring size in
  strata and in every tower-level analysis, so they must not be built from
  ring size. Ring size may check the types, but not define them. (The first
  draft used ring size inside the rules. Mark rejected it as muddying the
  concept.)
- *Split the villages.* An earlier draft put most towers in one village
  class. Mark: "I just don't feel like it's likely to distinguish between the
  isolated and low-population villages likely to have empty churches and the
  more typical ones."
- *Follow the settlement's own shape.* St Albans and Staines both sit near
  London, but feel completely different: there are "clear gaps between the
  city (/large town) and the ones around it" at St Albans, while Staines
  "felt like suburban spread".
- *Pay fair heed to 1988* as a guide to how to carve up the towers, starting
  with how many fell in each of its five types.
- *Check against towers people know.* A curated list in
  `data/reference/known_towers.csv` records, for each known tower, what sort
  of place it feels like.
- *Work outside England without rework*, and be meaningful to ringers.
- *Identify tower clusters* (Mark, 11 October), where towers stand close
  together and bands are shared, by a measure rather than only a list.
  Richard Heys's register shows several central Bristol ten-bell towers with
  no registered ringers, because they are rung by a cluster band.
- *Give no offence.* People will look up their own town on the map. A town
  whose central church is called a suburb, or a city denied a prestigious
  title its neighbour has, will feel slighted (Mark's father, 11 October).
  So the names are neutral, every settlement has a centre, and clusters of
  towers are a flag, not a rank.
- *Keep Bristol on the conurbation side* of any conurbation line.

**What this chapter does not decide.** The final types, their thresholds,
and the handling of the special-case towers. All are open questions in the
decision register (Q-022, Q-023).

## Headline findings

- **1988's types, by inference, held about
  `r pct(village_88)` villages, `r pct(counts_1988$share_best[4])` towns,
  `r pct(counts_1988$share_best[2])` suburban, `r pct(counts_1988$share_best[3])`
  large-city and `r pct(counts_1988$share_best[1])` inner-city towers.** The
  report does not publish the counts. They can be worked out, within narrow
  ranges, from its table of shared bands.
- **The first place-only draft (Draft A) had too many villages.** It put
  `r pct(village_a)` of comparable towers in villages, against 1988's
  `r pct(village_88)`, and could not tell St Albans from Staines.
- **Draft B ran aground on finding town centres.** It started from the
  settlement the tower stands in, which works. But population density could
  not find centres, because centres are short of residents; the share of
  non-residential buildings did better, but still missed absorbed town
  centres and promoted suburbs next to industrial estates. Its 500 m kernel
  also made some villages into towns.
- **The working draft (Draft C) finds centres by their high streets.** A
  tower inside a continuous built-up area of 50,000 or more is in a centre
  if it is within `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m of a District Centre or
  larger. On the test cases it misplaces
  `r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "centres made suburbs")` of `r sum(is_test_centre)`
  centres and `r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "suburbs made centres")` of
  `r sum(is_test_suburb)` suburbs, against
  `r ct("Non-residential share of buildings, against its built-up area's (Draft B)", "centres made suburbs")`
  and
  `r ct("Non-residential share of buildings, against its built-up area's (Draft B)", "suburbs made centres")`
  for Draft B's rule.
- **Towns and villages by the walkable population.** Outside cities, people
  per km² of land within a short walk (the 250 m kernel) decides. It keeps
  villages near a town, such as Datchworth and Tewin, as villages. In the
  Gloucester & Bristol register, it is also the scale at which density best
  tells towers with a band from towers without one (chapter *Towers and the
  places they stand in*).
- **Draft C's shares are close to 1988's.** Mapped onto 1988's five types,
  it puts `r pct(village_c)` of comparable towers in villages and
  `r pct(town_c)` in towns, against 1988's `r pct(village_88)` and
  `r pct(town_88)`.
- **It flags tower clusters by measure.** `r sum(frame_towers$tower_cluster)` frame
  towers have `r fmt(DRAFT_C$cluster_towers)` or more towers within 1 km, or
  are on the special list.
- **It splits the villages.** `r pct(type_share[["Small village or hamlet"]])`
  of frame towers are in a small village or hamlet, under
  `r fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density)` people per km² of land within a short
  walk. Only `r pct(p8_of("Small village or hamlet"))` of them have 8 or more
  bells, against `r pct(p8_of("Village"))` in larger villages.
- **It matches `r sum(known_c$agree)` of `r nrow(known_c)` known towers.**
  St Albans and Staines fall apart as Mark described.
  `r misses <- known_c$display[!known_c$agree]; if (length(misses) > 0) paste0("Misses: ", paste(misses, collapse = "; "), ".") else ""`

## How 1988 classified places

**The types.** The 1988 survey analysed its towers by five settlement types:
"Inner City of major conurbations, Suburban, Large City, Town,
Village".^[Central Council Survey of Ringing (1988), Chapter 9.] The
published account names the types but does not say how towers were assigned
to them. The analysis was done by Ron Johnston at the University of
Sheffield, a human geographer and a ringer who later became President of the
Central Council.^[Wikipedia, "Ron Johnston (geographer)".] The five types
follow the urban geography of the time, in particular its distinction
between the deprived inner city and the city centre.

**How many towers were in each type.** The report never gives the counts,
but Table 11.2 allows them to be worked out. It gives two figures for each
settlement type. In its words, "the first figure indicates the percentage of
towers with shared bands that are in the relevant category; the second
figure (in brackets) indicates the percentage within that specific category
that have shared bands". There were 47 towers with shared bands: "This gives
a total of 47 towers out of the sampled 500". So:

1. The first figure, applied to the 47, gives the number of shared bands in
   each type. Only one whole number fits each percentage.
2. Dividing by the second figure gives the number of towers in the type.
   Rounding leaves a range.
3. Where Table 9.1's percentages fit only one count within the range, that
   count is taken as the best estimate.

The text confirms the smallest: "half of the small number of inner city
towers were reported as having shared bands", which is 4 of 8.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-1988-counts
counts_1988 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `1988 type` = .data$type_1988,
    `% of the 47 shared bands` = .data$shared_pct_of_47,
    `shared bands` = .data$shared,
    `% of type with a shared band` = .data$pct_within,
    `towers in type` = ifelse(.data$n_min == .data$n_max, as.character(.data$n_min),
                              paste0(.data$n_min, "–", .data$n_max)),
    `best estimate` = .data$n_best,
    share = ifelse(pct(.data$share_lo) == pct(.data$share_hi), pct(.data$share_best), paste0(pct(.data$share_best), " (", pct(.data$share_lo), "–", pct(.data$share_hi), ")"))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "1988's towers by settlement type, inferred from Table 11.2 (share: best estimate, with the range rounding allows)")
```

**How far to trust these.** Four cautions apply.

- *They total about `r fmt(sum(counts_1988$n_best))` towers, not 500.* The
  survey had returns for 471 towers. The rest were apparently not
  classified, or not counted in this table. If they were mostly of one type,
  the shares would shift.
- *1988 was itself a sample.* With about 400 towers, a share near half is
  uncertain by about 5 percentage points either way (95% interval).
- *The frame was rings of five or more.* 1988 drew "500, picked at random
  from all of the towers listed in an updated computer version of Dove's
  guide", from "some 5425 towers with five or more bells". Comparisons below
  therefore use British Isles frame towers with five or more bells.
- *The assignment rule is unknown.* Similar shares are encouraging, but they
  do not show that a tower would have been placed in the same type.

1988's rates by type, for reference:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-1988-rates
rates_1988 |>
  dplyr::rename(`1988 type` = "type_1988",
                `% rung on survey Sunday` = "rung_pct",
                `% with a band` = "band_pct",
                `ringers per bell (towers with a band)` = "ringers_per_bell") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "1988's published rates by settlement type (Tables 9.1–9.3)")
```

In the survey's words, "the inner city and village church bells [are] much
more likely to be silent", and "the village and inner-city bands tend to be
the smallest".

## The ready-made classifications

Two official classifications are carried alongside the measures as
yardsticks. Both classify *areas*, not towers, and each was built to answer a
different question from ours. Knowing how they are made explains where they
fit ringing and where they do not.

| | Degree of Urbanisation (international) | ONS Rural Urban Classification 2021 | Scottish Government Urban Rural Classification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Covers | Every country | England and Wales | Scotland |
| Built from | 1 km population grid cells | Output Areas, about 125 households each | Settlements |
| Main idea | Size and density of contiguous built-up clusters | Address density and the population of the built-up area | Settlement population, plus drive time to a town of 10,000 |
| Classes | 3 at level 1, 7 at level 2 | 3 settlement classes x 2 access classes | 6 or 8 |
| Used here | Yes, for every tower | Yes, England and Wales only | No |

### The international Degree of Urbanisation

**Purpose.** One definition of city, town and rural area that works the same
in every country, so countries can be compared. The UN Statistical
Commission endorsed it in March 2020. Six bodies developed it: the European
Commission, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, UN-Habitat, the
International Labour Organization, the OECD and the World Bank. It is meant
to sit beside national definitions, not replace them: in the manual's words,
it "is intended to complement and not replace the definitions used by
national statistical offices".

**Construction.** It starts from a grid of 1 km cells with a population
count in each, ignoring administrative boundaries.

- **Urban centre:** a contiguous patch of cells with at least 1,500 people
  per km² and at least 50,000 people in total, joined edge to edge.
- **Urban cluster:** a contiguous patch with at least 300 people per km² and
  at least 5,000 in total, joined edge to edge or corner to corner.
- **Rural:** everything else.

Level 2 splits these further, into seven classes: urban centre; dense and
semi-dense urban clusters; suburban or peri-urban cells; and three rural
classes by density. Access to services is left out on purpose, so that
access can be studied separately.

**What it means for ringing.** It is the only scheme that works unchanged
for the Australian and US towers. Taken cell by cell, each tower simply
takes the class of the 1 km cell it falls in, so a tower near a cell edge
can take a class that does not match its own street. Its urban centres,
traced as whole patches, are more robust, and Draft C uses them. This
project uses its GHSL implementation (the EU's Global Human Settlement
Layer, 2020 epoch).

### The ONS Rural Urban Classification 2021

**Purpose.** The official urban–rural split for statistics and policy in
England and Wales. The basic unit is the Output Area.

**Construction.** In ONS's words, Output Areas are "defined as 'Urban' if
they have a high density of residential addresses, or if they intersect with
Amalgamated Built Up Areas (ABUAs) with a resident population of 10,000 or
more". An Amalgamated Built Up Area joins built-up areas "within 200m of one
another and with a direct road connection, representing larger
conurbations". Everything else is rural, split into Larger and Smaller rural.
Each class is then split by "relative access": nearer to or further from a
major town or city of more than 75,000 people, by travel time.

**What it means for ringing.** Because built-up areas within 200 m are
joined, a whole conurbation becomes one urban area. With three settlement
classes it is also coarse. The 2021 and 2011 versions are not directly
comparable, because the method changed.

**Its predecessor is closer to this project's approach.** The 2011
classification had ten classes, including "Major Conurbation", "Minor
Conurbation", "Town and Fringe", "Village" and "Hamlets and Isolated
Dwellings". It recognised settlement *form*. Each dwelling was placed in a
100 m cell, and density was measured at several increasing distances around
it to build a "density profile". That is the same idea as this project's
kernels.

### Scotland and Northern Ireland

Scotland has its own classification. It is based on settlement population
(Large Urban Areas of 125,000 or more, Other Urban Areas of 10,000 to
124,999, Small Towns of 3,000 to 9,999, and Rural Areas below 3,000) and on
drive time to a settlement of 10,000 or more. Northern Ireland has a separate
settlement classification from NISRA. Neither is loaded here: Dove lists only
24 Scottish rings, and treats the island of Ireland as a single country.

### Why none is enough on its own

Each answers "how urban is this area?" for its own territory. Ringing needs
one answer that works for every tower, follows the settlement rather than an
administrative area, and separates a free-standing city from a suburb. Draft
B borrows from all three: the Degree of Urbanisation's urban centres and
village size, and the Scottish scheme's idea of a small town.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-smod-ruc
frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$ruc21nm)) |>
  dplyr::count(.data$ruc21nm, .data$smod_class) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "smod_class", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "England & Wales frame towers: ONS RUC 2021 against Degree of Urbanisation")
```

## Draft A, and why it was set aside

**What it did.** Draft A measured each tower's own settlement with a 1 km
circle (village, town, or city and large town, on the Degree of
Urbanisation's density and population lines), and crossed that with whether
the region within the 8 km kernel was built-up.

**Why it was set aside.** Three problems, found by Mark against towers he
knows and by comparison with 1988:

- *Too many villages, all alike.* It put `r pct(village_a)` of comparable
  towers in one village class, against 1988's `r pct(village_88)`. It had no
  way to pick out the small, isolated villages most likely to have empty
  churches.
- *It could not see gaps between settlements.* A "built-up region" line on
  the 8 km kernel counts everyone nearby, whether or not they live in the
  same place. St Albans and Staines both came out as "city or large town in a
  conurbation".
- *A wide-area line is arbitrary.* Small moves in it moved hundreds of
  towers between classes.

## Draft B, and where it ran aground

**What it did** (D-029 to D-036). Draft B kept what Draft A lacked: it
started from the settlement the tower stands in. A tower in a continuous
built-up area of 50,000 or more was in that city or conurbation; elsewhere,
people per km² of land on a 500 m kernel made it a town (420 or more), a
village (200 to 420), or a small village or hamlet.

**Where it ran aground: finding centres.** Inside a city, Draft B had to say
which towers are at its centre and which in its suburbs, and nothing it
measured could do that well.

- *Population density cannot find a town centre.* Centres are short of
  residents, because shops and offices have replaced homes. Density lines
  made Wolverhampton's collegiate church, the minsters of Halifax, Rotherham
  and Hull, and many cathedrals into suburbs. Inside a conurbation they
  judged a town like Wolverhampton against the whole West Midlands, and
  London's average density was so far above any other city's that London
  needed a rule of its own.
- *The non-residential share of buildings did better, but not well enough*
  (D-036). A centre is where a town's shops and offices are, so the share
  of buildings that are not homes should find it. It did find most centres,
  but town centres absorbed into a larger built-up area fell short of that
  area's share (Stockport, Epsom, Pontefract, Leyland), and suburban churches
  next to an industrial estate came out central (Brockworth). The satellite
  layer it uses measures the ground buildings cover, so it cannot tell a
  high street from a warehouse.

**And a second problem: villages made into towns.** A 500 m kernel weighs
in people well over a kilometre away. Near a town, it counts the town's
edge as part of the village: Datchworth and Tewin, small Hertfordshire
villages a mile or two from Welwyn and Welwyn Garden City, came out as
towns. Draft B's check against the international urban clusters did not
catch this, because those clusters join such villages to the town next
door (see *Why the 250 m kernel*, below).

Draft C keeps Draft B's frame, and fixes both: centres by their high
streets, towns and villages by the walkable population.

## Draft C: start from the settlement, find its high streets

**The rules.**

*Outside a continuous built-up area of 50,000 or more*, the density of
people within a short walk of the church decides:

| Type | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Town | At least `r fmt(DRAFT_C$town_density)` people per km² of land |
| Village | `r fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density)` to `r fmt(DRAFT_C$town_density)` people per km² of land |
| Small village or hamlet | Under `r fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density)` people per km² of land |

*Inside one*, the tower is in a **centre** if either holds:

- it is on or near a high street: within `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m of
  a retail centre of District Centre size or larger (below). Abroad, where
  retail centres are not mapped, the buildings around the church must
  instead be at least as commercial as its built-up area as a whole: the
  non-residential share of the built-up surface, as in Draft B;
- it stands among old churches: `r fmt(DRAFT_C$old_centre_towers)` or more
  towers within 1 km, itself included.

If that leaves a built-up area with no centre at all, its most densely
populated tower is its centre, so every settlement has one. Every other tower
is in a **suburb**. The size of the built-up area names the type:

| Type | Built-up area |
| --- | --- |
| City or large town: centre, or suburb | `r fmt(50000)` to `r fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop)` people |
| Conurbation: centre, or suburb | `r fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop)` people or more |

*On top of its type*, a tower is flagged as in a **tower cluster** if it has
`r fmt(DRAFT_C$cluster_towers)` or more towers within 1 km, itself included,
or is on the special list as a society tower.

**The measures.**

- "Within a short walk" is the `r measure_label(LOCAL_VAR)`: the weight
  halves every 250 m, so it counts the people a few minutes' walk from the
  church. Population is divided by the land the kernel covers, so the sea
  does not count as empty country. The international Degree of
  Urbanisation's lines are 300 people per km² (a cluster, rural or urban)
  and 1,500 (an urban centre), in the same units.^[Whether the Degree of
  Urbanisation divides by land or by the whole 1 km cell has not been
  checked here. Inland the two are the same.]
- An **urban centre** is a continuous built-up area, traced on the Degree of
  Urbanisation's 1 km grid with its own rules: cells of at least 1,500 people
  per km², joined edge to edge, totalling at least 50,000 people.
- **Retail centres** are the CDRC's Retail Centre Boundaries for the UK
  (Open Government Licence; Goodwin and others, below): the outline of
  every cluster of shops, traced from Foursquare's business listings and
  OpenStreetMap land use, with candidate centres in "office parks, business
  trading estates and logistics facilities" removed. Each centre is classed
  by its rank within its region, local authority and built-up area, and by
  its number of retail units. Draft C ranks the high-street classes from
  Regional Centre (1), through Major Town Centre (2), Town Centre and Market
  Town (3), to District Centre (4), Local Centre (5) and Small Local Centre
  (6). Retail parks and shopping centres are left out: they are out-of-town
  destinations, not the centre of a place. A church inside an outline is at
  distance 0.
- **Buildings**, used abroad, come from the EU's Global Human Settlement
  Layer: built-up surface per 100 m cell, and its non-residential part
  (shops, offices, schools, hospitals, industry).

**Where each line comes from.** All are provisional, and the sensitivity
tables below show what moving them does.

- *Urban centre, 50,000 people:* the international definition, unchanged.
  Following the continuous built-up area is what separates St Albans, a city
  with its own centre, from Staines, which is part of London's.
- *Conurbation, `r fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop)` people:* set in a gap in
  the sizes of urban centres, so that a small change in the data cannot move
  a city across it (the table below lists the centres either side). It takes
  in London and the large metropolitan areas, which 1988 called the "major
  conurbations", and Bristol, as Mark wanted.
- *Centre, a District Centre or larger within `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m:*
  District Centres count because of how the CDRC ranks. A centre that does
  not lead its local authority or built-up area cannot be a Town Centre or
  Market Town, however old: such "sub-leading centres of comparable size"
  are District Centres, with at least 150 retail units. Old towns inside a
  larger authority or built-up area, among them Warwick and Dudley, are
  therefore District Centres; leaving them out would make those churches
  suburbs. Local Centres (100 to 150 units) are left out because many
  suburbs have a high street of that size. 250 m is a few
  minutes' walk from the edge of the high street. The table below compares
  the alternatives.
- *Old centre, `r fmt(DRAFT_C$old_centre_towers)` towers within 1 km:*
  keeps old centres of churches central, such as Gloucester's, whatever is
  built round them.
- *Tower cluster, `r fmt(DRAFT_C$cluster_towers)` towers within 1 km*
  (Mark, 11 October): towers close enough to walk between, so one band can
  ring several in a morning when service times allow. Counting towers, not
  bells, keeps ring size out (D-028). Counting the tower itself means towers
  all within 1 km of each other share one count, so a cluster is never split
  by its own rings: all five Norwich towers, Mancroft included, are in it.
- *Town, `r fmt(DRAFT_C$town_density)` people per km² of land:* close to the
  line that best matches 1988's share of towns
  (`r if (line_88 == DRAFT_C$town_density) "it is that line" else paste0(fmt(line_88), " on the same kernel")`).
  It sits between the international cluster line (300) and urban-centre
  line (1,500).
- *Village, `r fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density)` people per km² of land*
  (Mark, 11 October): below it are hamlets, and villages small enough to
  struggle for a band. The line is there so that "village" is not one
  monolithic class, not to mark a natural break. The international cluster
  line (300) would put
  `r pct(mean(reclass(frame_towers, village_density = 300) == "Small village or hamlet"))`
  of frame towers in small villages and hamlets and only
  `r pct(mean(reclass(frame_towers, village_density = 300) == "Village"))`
  in villages, so the larger type would carry the smaller name. At
  `r fmt(DRAFT_C$village_density)` the two are
  `r pct(type_share[["Small village or hamlet"]])` and
  `r pct(type_share[["Village"]])`.

### How centres are found

The test cases were chosen before either rule was settled: churches at the
heart of their towns, and churches in suburbs. The first three rules compare
the area round the church with its own built-up area as a whole; the rest
use the retail centres. The shares are of comparable towers in 1988's three
urban types (1988 itself: Large City 6%, Suburban 11%, Inner City 2%).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-centre-test
centre_test |>
  dplyr::mutate(`known towers agreeing` = paste(known_by_rule, "of", nrow(known_c))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Seven ways of finding centres: shares of comparable towers in 1988's urban types, test centres (", sum(is_test_centre), ") and test suburbs (", sum(is_test_suburb), ") misplaced, and known towers agreeing"))
```

**What the table shows.**

- *Density is the worst guide to a centre*, as Draft B found: it makes
  `r ct("People per km² of land, against its built-up area's", "centres made suburbs")`
  of the test centres into suburbs.
- *Retail centres do best on the test cases.* A District Centre or larger
  within `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m misplaces the fewest test towers of
  any rule that keeps all `r nrow(known_c)` known towers right, and its
  shares of 1988's urban types are close to 1988's.
- *Town Centres alone are too strict.* The CDRC classes some old town
  centres inside larger built-up areas as District Centres, so Warwick and
  Dudley become suburbs.
- *400 m is too generous.* It recovers two more test centres, but makes
  Staines `r tolower(staines_at("District Centre or larger within 400 m"))`,
  where Mark knows it as suburban.
- *Counting Local Centres too is a close call.* On the test cases it does
  as well (`r ct("Local Centre or larger within 250 m", "centres made suburbs")`
  centres and `r ct("Local Centre or larger within 250 m", "suburbs made centres")`
  suburbs misplaced), but it makes `r n_extra_local` more towers central
  and moves the suburban share further from 1988's. The extra towers are a
  mix: small towns swallowed by a larger built-up area (Colne, Bedworth,
  Elland, Willenhall) and suburbs round an old village high street (Cheam,
  Jesmond, Stoke Newington, Westbury on Trym). The test suburbs were picked
  as plainly suburban, so they cannot settle it. Draft C keeps the stricter
  rule.

**Its weak points.**

- *Churches set back from the high street.*
  `r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "the centres")` stand more than
  `r DRAFT_C$centre_retail_m` m from a District Centre or larger: the
  shopping has moved away from the old church (Hastings Old Town), or the
  CDRC files the place's high street as a smaller centre. One is arguably a
  mislabelled test case: Stockport's market-place church, S Mary, is a
  centre; S George stands about a kilometre out, on Buxton Road.
- *Suburbs with a large high street of their own*
  (`r ct(CHOSEN_RULE, "the suburbs")`): these are arguably centres. Dunstable
  is a town in its own right, joined to Luton's built-up area.
- *UK only.* Abroad the non-residential share decides, with its known
  weaknesses. `r pct(mean(!dplyr::coalesce(frame_towers$retail_covered, FALSE)))`
  of frame towers are outside the CDRC's coverage.
- *A snapshot.* The boundaries come from recent business listings, and
  high streets change slowly, but they do change. A newer release should
  be checked before the draw.

### Why the 250 m kernel for towns and villages

**The principle** (Mark, 11 October). The types describe places as they are
today, for today's bands. The question for a village is how many people live
close enough to walk to its church, not how many live within a few miles.

**Why Draft B chose 500 m, and why that check misled.** Draft B checked
each scale against the international urban clusters (contiguous patches of
300 people per km² or more, totalling 5,000+), which are traced without any
kernel. Each kernel's town line is set to match 1988's share of towns:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-town-scale
town_scale |>
  dplyr::transmute(kernel = .data$kernel,
                   `town line matching 1988 (people per km² of land)` = fmt(.data$line),
                   `"Town" agrees with being in an urban cluster` = pct(.data$agree)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Towns at four scales: agreement with the contiguous urban clusters (5,000+ people), British Isles frame towers outside urban centres")
```

Wider kernels do well on this test, but the test rewards blurring. Urban
clusters are traced on 1 km cells joined corner to corner, so a village
whose cells touch a town's joins its cluster: the cluster that takes in
Codicote and Tewin is London's, with millions of people. A
kernel that also blurs the village into the town agrees with the cluster,
for the same wrong reason.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-herts
herts |>
  dplyr::transmute(tower = .data$display,
                   `250 m` = fmt(.data$density_land_k250m),
                   `500 m` = fmt(.data$density_land_k500m),
                   `1 km` = fmt(.data$density_land_k1km),
                   `2 km` = fmt(.data$density_land_k2km),
                   `urban cluster (people)` = ifelse(is.na(.data$urban_pop), "none", fmt(.data$urban_pop)),
                   `Draft C` = as.character(.data$type)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Three Hertfordshire villages and Welwyn: people per km² of land on each kernel")
```

**What the villages show.** Within a short walk, Datchworth and Tewin are
villages, and Codicote, a large village with a high street of its own, is
a town. From 500 m outwards, the edges of Welwyn and Welwyn Garden City are
counted in: Datchworth and Tewin rise above Draft B's town line, while
Welwyn itself, a compact old town, falls. People who know them call
Datchworth and Tewin villages.

**What the bands show.** In the Gloucester & Bristol register, the 250 m
kernel is also the scale at which density best separates towers with a band
from towers without one, and the fit worsens steadily as the kernel widens
(chapter *Towers and the places they stand in*). This is one Association,
and the scale was chosen partly on it, so the census's own data should
re-test it.

**What the wider density still tells.** Two villages of the same size can be
alone in open country or a mile from a town. The density beyond a short walk
(`beyond_walk`, the people between the 250 m and 2 km kernels per km² of
their land) measures that. It is not a type: in the register it added
nothing to the walkable density. It sorts the draw within each stratum, so
the sample spreads from isolated villages to those near towns.

### How the shares compare with 1988

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shares-1988
shares_vs_1988 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `1988 type` = .data$type_1988,
    `1988 (inferred)` = ifelse(pct(.data$share_lo) == pct(.data$share_hi), pct(.data$share_best), paste0(pct(.data$share_best), " (", pct(.data$share_lo), "–", pct(.data$share_hi), ")")),
    `Draft A` = pct(.data$draft_a),
    `Draft C` = pct(.data$draft_c)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Shares of towers by 1988 type: 1988 inferred, against both drafts on comparable towers (British Isles frame, five or more bells, n = ", fmt(nrow(comparable_1988)), ")"))
```

Draft C maps onto 1988's types as follows: both village types to Village;
Town to Town; a city or large town's centre to Large City; either kind of
suburb to Suburban; a conurbation's centre to Inner City; and any tower in a
tower cluster to Large City, because 1988's "Large City" was the type of the
great city-centre churches: the most ringers per bell, and the most Surprise
ringing.

**Where Draft C still differs from 1988.** Two gaps remain.

- *Towns and villages.* `r if (line_88 == DRAFT_C$town_density) "The town line was chosen to match 1988's share of towns, so this gap is closed by construction. That makes the match a choice, not evidence that the two schemes place the same towers alike." else paste0("1988 seems to have called more places towns. A town line of ", fmt(line_88), " per km² would match 1988's share.")`
- *Fewer suburbs.* Draft C has fewer suburban towers than 1988. 1988 may
  have counted some fringe towns as suburban; and Draft C makes every
  settlement's densest tower a centre where nothing else qualifies.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-types
frame_towers |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    towers   = dplyr::n(),
    share    = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(dplyr::n() / nrow(frame_towers)),
    `median people within 1 km` = fmt(stats::median(.data$pop_r1km)),
    `median people per km² (2 km kernel)` = fmt(stats::median(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]])),
    `median bells` = stats::median(.data$bells),
    .by = "type"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$type) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Draft C types, all frame towers")
```

### Independent checks

Ring size and "growth since the bells" play no part in the rules. If the
types mean something, both should still change steadily from type to type.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ring-check
ring_check |>
  dplyr::mutate(`rings of 8 or more` = pct(.data$p8)) |>
  dplyr::select(-"p8") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Ring size and growth since the bells, by Draft C type (neither is used to classify)")
```

**What the checks show.** Rings of 8 or more rise from
`r pct(p8_of("Small village or hamlet"))` in small villages and hamlets, to
`r pct(p8_of("Village"))` in villages and `r pct(p8_of("Town"))` in towns.
The village split is therefore real in the one outcome available before the
census: small villages are much less likely to have a large ring. Whether
they are also more likely to have no band, as Mark expects, is for the
census to show. 1988 found that only 70% of village towers had a band,
against 92% of towns, so the gap may well sit mostly in the smallest places.

### Sense check: towers people know

The types should feel right for towers people know well. Each person records
what sort of place a tower feels like, in the types' own words, and the table
compares that with the rules.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-known
known_c |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    tower = .data$display,
    `feels like` = .data$feels_like,
    `Draft C` = as.character(.data$type),
    match = ifelse(.data$agree, "yes", "**no**"),
    `Draft A` = as.character(.data$type_a),
    `people within 500 m` = fmt(.data$pop_r500m),
    `people per km² of land within a short walk` = fmt(.data[[LOCAL_VAR]]),
    `nearest retail centre` = ifelse(is.na(.data$retail_nearest_name), "",
                                     paste0(sub(";.*$", "", .data$retail_nearest_name), " (", .data$retail_nearest_class, ", ",
                                            fmt(.data$retail_nearest_m), " m)")),
    `District Centre or larger (m)` = fmt(.data$retail_d_t4_m),
    `tower cluster` = ifelse(.data$tower_cluster, "yes", ""),
    `urban centre (people)` = ifelse(is.na(.data$centre_pop), "none", fmt(.data$centre_pop)),
    `nearest urban centre (km)` = round(.data$centre_dist_km, 1),
    `international class` = as.character(.data$smod_class)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Known towers: how they feel, and how the drafts class them")
```

`r if (n_known_missing > 0) paste0("**", n_known_missing, " known towers were not found** among the ringable towers; check their tower IDs.") else ""`

**What the known towers show.**

- **St Albans and Staines now fall apart, as they feel.** St Albans has its
  own urban centre of `r fmt(st_albans$centre_pop)` people, separated from
  London by green belt. Staines is inside London's urban centre of
  `r fmt(staines$centre_pop)`. This is the distinction Draft A could not draw.
- **Oxford, York and the City of London are centres, and in tower
  clusters.** As they feel: the cluster flag sits on top of the type, so
  these towers are still "a city".
- **Amersham and Welwyn are both towns, as they feel.** Amersham has
  `r fmt(amersham[[LOCAL_VAR]])` people per km² of land around the church,
  Welwyn `r fmt(welwyn[[LOCAL_VAR]])`; each sits about
  `r round(mean(c(amersham$centre_dist_km, welwyn$centre_dist_km)))` km from
  the nearest urban centre. They are twins: historic towns of equal size and
  standing, each now beside a larger, newer neighbour (Amersham-on-the-Hill,
  Welwyn Garden City), and both St Mary's.

More known towers, especially outside the South East, would show whether
cases like these are rare or common.

### Urban centres near the conurbation line

The conurbation line sits in a gap between urban-centre sizes. The tables
list the centres either side, with the places that have most frame towers
in each, so that a re-run which moves a city across the line is visible.
The line was chosen on UK cities, so they come first; a few centres
elsewhere follow, to show how the line reads abroad.

```{r}
#| label: centres-prep
#| include: false
centre_names <- towers |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$centre_pop), .data$in_frame) |>
  dplyr::mutate(place = sub(",.*$", "", .data$display),
                place = sub(" (Cath|Minster|Abbey|Priory)\\b.*$", "", .data$place)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(towers_include = paste(utils::head(names(sort(table(.data$place), decreasing = TRUE)), 3),
                                         collapse = ", "),
                   uk = mean(.data$uk) > 0.5,
                   country = names(sort(table(.data$country), decreasing = TRUE))[1],
                   `frame towers` = dplyr::n(), .by = "centre_key") |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::distinct(dplyr::select(towers, "centre_key", "centre_pop")), by = "centre_key")
centre_table <- function(d) d |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(.data$centre_pop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(side = ifelse(.data$centre_pop >= DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop,
                              "conurbation", "city or large town"),
                people = fmt(.data$centre_pop))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-centres-uk
centre_names |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$uk,
                .data$centre_pop >= DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop / 2,
                .data$centre_pop <= DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop * 2) |>
  centre_table() |>
  dplyr::select(`frame towers include` = "towers_include", "people", "frame towers", "side") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("UK urban centres between half and twice the conurbation line of ",
                                fmt(DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop), " people"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-centres-abroad
centre_names |>
  dplyr::filter(!.data$uk) |>
  centre_table() |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |>
  dplyr::select("country", `frame towers include` = "towers_include", "people", "frame towers", "side") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "The largest urban centres with frame towers outside the UK")
```

### Tower clusters

```{r}
#| label: tbl-clusters
clusters <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$tower_cluster) |>
  dplyr::mutate(place = sub(",.*$", "", .data$display),
                place = sub(" (Cath|Minster|Abbey|Priory)\\b.*$", "", .data$place),
                by = ifelse(.data$towers_1km >= DRAFT_C$cluster_towers, "measure", "list only"))
clusters |>
  dplyr::summarise(towers = dplyr::n(),
                   `found by the measure` = sum(.data$by == "measure"),
                   `on the special list` = sum(.data$society),
                   .by = "place") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(.data$towers)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers in tower clusters, by place")
```

**What it shows.** `r nrow(clusters)` frame towers are in a tower cluster.
The measure finds `r sum(clusters$by == "measure")` of them without any list,
including `r sum(clusters$by == "measure" & clusters$society)` of the
`r sum(frame_towers$society)` towers on the special list. The list adds
`r sum(clusters$by == "list only")` more.

**Why a flag, not a type.** A type named for prestige ("historic city core")
invites comparison: a city left out would feel slighted, and towers inside
it would read as grander than their neighbours (Mark, 11 October). A cluster
of towers is a plain fact about the place, and it matters for bands, which
can be shared across towers within walking distance. On the map, clusters
are drawn with a bold outline over their ordinary type.

**Why towers, counting the tower itself.** An earlier version counted bells
at *other* towers. That split Norwich's cluster: Mancroft, with the largest
ring, had the fewest other bells nearby and fell outside while its
neighbours, counting Mancroft's twelve, were in. Counting towers, the tower
included, gives towers all within 1 km of each other the same count. It also
keeps ring size out of the flag.

### Centres and suburbs: test cases

**Why suburbs matter.** In 1988, "Suburban" probably covered the suburbs of
smaller cities as well as of conurbations. Mark's view, from Gloucester and
Cheltenham: the eights out at the edges make sense as suburban, in the orbit
of the city as villages are in the orbit of a conurbation. His prior, not
yet tested: the more ambitious ringers cross between city and suburb bands,
while less experienced members keep to their suburb. The census's own
question on where people rang in census week (D-030) could test that.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-suburb-tests
test_places <- c("Gloucester", "Cheltenham", "Barnwood", "Quedgeley", "Brockworth",
                 "Upton St Leonards", "Charlton Kings", "Leckhampton", "Prestbury",
                 "Luton", "Dunstable", "Wakefield", "Batley", "Dewsbury",
                 "St Albans", "Exeter", "Norwich", "Watford", "Staines", "Kingston upon Thames",
                 "Wolverhampton", "Halifax", "Stockport")
frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$centre_pop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(place = sub(",.*$", "", .data$display),
                place = sub(" (Cath|Minster|Abbey|Priory|Collegiate)\\b.*$", "", .data$place)) |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$place %in% test_places) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$centre_pop, .data$retail_d_t4_m) |>
  dplyr::transmute(`built-up area (people)` = fmt(.data$centre_pop), tower = .data$display,
                   `nearest retail centre` = paste0(sub(";.*$", "", .data$retail_nearest_name), " (",
                                                    .data$retail_nearest_class, ")"),
                   `District Centre or larger (m)` = fmt(.data$retail_d_t4_m),
                   `non-residential ratio` = round(.data$nres_ratio, 2),
                   `towers within 1 km` = .data$towers_1km,
                   `Draft C` = as.character(.data$type),
                   cluster = ifelse(.data$tower_cluster, "yes", "")) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Test cases: towers in built-up areas, with the measures behind centre and suburb")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fallback
fallback <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$centre_pop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(by_rule = dplyr::coalesce(.data$retail_near,
                                          .data$nres_ratio >= DRAFT_C$centre_nres_ratio, FALSE) |
                  .data$towers_1km >= DRAFT_C$old_centre_towers) |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$british_isles) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rule_finds_centre = any(.data$by_rule),
                   place = sub(",.*$", "", .data$display[which.max(.data[[LOCAL_VAR]])]),
                   people = dplyr::first(.data$centre_pop), towers = dplyr::n(),
                   .by = "centre_key") |>
  dplyr::filter(!.data$rule_finds_centre)
```

**Every settlement has a centre.** In `r nrow(fallback)` built-up areas in the British Isles the
rule finds no centre, so the most densely populated tower is its centre.
Most are towns with one or two towers, such as
`r paste(utils::head(fallback$place[order(-fallback$people)], 5), collapse = ", ")`.
The fallback picks by residents, so where a town's old centre is empty it
can pick a suburb instead. In the UK, a built-up area that reaches this
fallback usually has no high street of District Centre size near any of its
towers.

### How sensitive the types are to each line

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-town
purrr::map(sort(unique(c(400, 500, DRAFT_C$town_density, 700, 800))), \(t)
  frame_towers |> dplyr::mutate(type = reclass(frame_towers, town_density = t)) |>
    dplyr::count(.data$type) |> dplyr::mutate(line = fmt(t))) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "line", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers per type at different town lines (people per km² of land within a short walk)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-village
purrr::map(sort(unique(c(150, DRAFT_C$village_density, 250, 300, 400))), \(t)
  frame_towers |> dplyr::mutate(type = reclass(frame_towers, village_density = t)) |>
    dplyr::count(.data$type) |> dplyr::mutate(line = fmt(t))) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "line", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers per type at different village lines (people per km² of land within a short walk)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-urban
dplyr::bind_rows(
  purrr::map(sort(unique(c(250000, 500000, DRAFT_C$conurbation_pop, 1000000))), \(t)
    frame_towers |> dplyr::mutate(type = reclass(frame_towers, conurbation_pop = t)) |>
      dplyr::count(.data$type) |> dplyr::mutate(line = paste("conurbation", fmt(t)))) |>
    purrr::list_rbind(),
  purrr::map(sort(unique(c(0.8, DRAFT_C$centre_nres_ratio, 1.2))), \(t)
    frame_towers |> dplyr::mutate(type = reclass(frame_towers, centre_nres_ratio = t)) |>
      dplyr::count(.data$type) |> dplyr::mutate(line = paste("ratio abroad", t))) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "line", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers per type at different conurbation sizes (people), and different non-residential ratios (used abroad only)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-retail
tidyr::expand_grid(tier = 3:5, m = c(0, 150, 250, 400)) |>
  purrr::pmap(\(tier, m) frame_towers |>
    dplyr::mutate(type = reclass(frame_towers, centre_retail_tier = tier, centre_retail_m = m)) |>
    dplyr::summarise(`centre towers` = sum(grepl("centre", .data$type)),
                     `suburb towers` = sum(grepl("suburb", .data$type))) |>
    dplyr::mutate(`retail centres counted` = c("Town Centre or larger", "District Centre or larger",
                                               "Local Centre or larger")[tier - 2],
                  `within (m)` = m)) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  dplyr::relocate("retail centres counted", "within (m)") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers in centres and suburbs, by the retail centres counted and how near the church must be (0: inside the outline)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-cluster
tibble::tibble(`towers within 1 km` = 3:7) |>
  dplyr::mutate(`frame towers flagged` = purrr::map_int(.data$`towers within 1 km`, \(n)
    sum(tower_cluster(frame_towers$towers_1km, frame_towers$society,
                      utils::modifyList(DRAFT_C, list(cluster_towers = n)))))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers in a tower cluster at different lines")
```

**What moves and what does not.** The village and town lines trade towers
between neighbouring rural types, as expected. The urban types depend
only on the conurbation line and the retail rule (the non-residential ratio
matters only abroad). The total in urban
centres depends on none of them, because the urban centres themselves are
fixed by the international definition.

### Examples and maps

Five towers drawn at random from each type, to test whether the names fit:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-type-examples
frame_towers |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$british_isles) |>

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-type-map
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-cap: "Draft C types, Great Britain."
gb <- dplyr::filter(frame_towers, .data$country %in% c("England", "Wales", "Scotland"))
ggplot(gb, aes(lon, lat, colour = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_TYPE, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3), nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-type-zoom
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Draft C types around London, the West Midlands and Manchester."
zooms <- tibble::tribble(
  ~area,            ~lon_min, ~lon_max, ~lat_min, ~lat_max,
  "London",           -0.55,     0.35,    51.25,    51.85,
  "West Midlands",    -2.35,    -1.55,    52.30,    52.70,
  "Manchester",       -2.55,    -1.95,    53.30,    53.65
)
zoomed <- purrr::pmap(zooms, \(area, lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max)
  frame_towers |>
    dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(.data$lon, lon_min, lon_max),
                  dplyr::between(.data$lat, lat_min, lat_max)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(area = area)) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
ggplot(zoomed, aes(lon, lat, colour = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_TYPE, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~area, scales = "free") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3), nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

## Methods and sources

**1988.** *The Central Council Survey of Ringing* (1988 survey, published in
*The Ringing World* 1989 and collected as a book). Chapter 2 (sampling),
Chapter 9 (geography, Tables 9.1–9.3), Chapter 11 (shared bands, Table
11.2). Ron Johnston: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Johnston_(geographer).

**Degree of Urbanisation.** Eurostat (2021), *Applying the Degree of
Urbanisation: a methodological manual to define cities, towns and rural areas
for international comparisons*. UN Statistical Commission endorsement, March
2020. GHS-SMOD R2023A and GHS-POP R2023A: Schiavina, M. et al. (2023),
European Commission Joint Research Centre.

**ONS Rural Urban Classification.** ONS, *The 2021 Rural Urban
Classification* (methodology and user guide). Defra/ONS, *The 2011
Rural-Urban Classification for Output Areas in England: user guide* (2013).

**Scotland.** Scottish Government, *Urban Rural Classification 2022:
methodology*.

**Retail centres.** Goodwin, O., Yin, Z., Ye, Z., Singleton, A. and Dolega,
L., *An Open Framework for Delineating and Classifying Retail Centres across
the United Kingdom* (working paper, with the data). Retail Centre
Boundaries (UK), Geographic Data Service / Consumer Data Research Centre,
https://data.geods.ac.uk/dataset/retail-centre-boundaries, Open Government
Licence; downloaded 11 October 2026.
